comments.author: @vibinginthecorner
comments.text:
Claude is my go-to. But for tasks like analyzing large amounts of data, extracting data from images, or anything that's going to require a huge context window, Gemini comes in clutch. 

Gemini is really good at not overcomplicating things. Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all want to write code for everything. Gemini will just use thinking/reasoning instead, which can be better for certain things. 

Today I took some screenshots of stock market data and asked both ChatGPT and Grok to analyze it. GPT failed miserably, overcomplicating things and somehow getting the math wrong, even though it used Python to do it. Grok was a little better, but still needed some coaxing in the right direction and wanted to overcomplicate things by writing code to analyze a very small dataset (a table with 40 rows and 3 columns). Gemini understood the assignment and did exactly the analysis I wanted, no code, wrote a concise but thorough report, and added in some good insights I hadn't thought about. Also, no fluff and chatter with Gemini. Straight to the point. 

Gemini is less sycophantic, in my opinion. Claude says every idea I have is brilliant. I can assure you, that is not the case. 😂 

Anyway, thank you for this timely video. I look forward to using the new Claude, even if I do sometimes cheat on him with my side-guy, Gemini. (Shhhh!)

comments.text: its getting better but its not there yet.  I am still finding extensive debugging is required and "looped errors" some models can't find their own errors but other models can find errors to help other models fix their errors. I think once more agentic problem solving occurs. Like the AI is still providing solutions that are build errors if the models actually were able to test code builds before suggesting it then it would be a better system 1. build code 2. test code. if code does not build 3. gather possible reasons why code isn't building from other models by designing ideale prompts for problem analysis 4. test suggestions if suggestions build remember solutions for future builds.  Currently they think code will work that doesn't. That is a fatal error imo. The models are still very error prone. improving yes but they don't check with other models for solution and this is often the fastest way to find a fix. I find kimi is good at finding errors but isn't very good at programming in general.  Claude can sometimes fix code but other times doesn't.  Grok can often code and fix code but has the tendency to rewite graphical elements and isn't very good at graphics.   Gemini isn't very good at coding in general but is great at graphics design. ChatGPT can often get concepts done very well but takes a lot more work than say Grok to get code working.  IMO they all have their own strengths and weaknesses and the models are far more better working as a group than individually to get code working.

We are reaching a point where I imagine there will start to be dramatic effects on work. At the same time, I wonder how far it can go without some kinds of unsustainable internal issues.

If AIs can do real work that passes the Turing test, and do it in much less time, companies will need far fewer people to work in those cubicles. And I don't think this will just be about young professionals, 22 - 26 years old. I can't imagine companies continuing to hire enough people to fill the need for employment when they have this kind of AI capability. And if this happens, aren't there going to be fewer people making enough money to pay the high subscription rates of AI services?

If we can use AIs to read and create our emails, for example, how long will it be before it's just AIs talking to each other? Relationships will be spouses just using their "agents" to carry on most of the communication in their relationships. In business, it will just be AIs sending reports and documents to each other.

Idk, I've been saying for years as they scale they'll start using machine code. It is code. Fundumentally it's not a different kind of code. You can decompile it directly into ASM, all the "high level" code is just functions of that. Compilers today are pretty complex in an attempt to optimize code, but they use to just replace your code with machine code, it's the same thing. Idk why anyone thinks this is different than writing code.

The only other thing I think it could be doing is a kind of modularized 2d "world builder", it doesn't execute code, it just has AI update the screen with what it thinks it should be doing, but that would be salllloooooooow.

I do think AI written UI is a next step. An application is just the functions, and then you tell it what features you want access too, you can move UI elements around. Ask to to add or remove UI, change the color scheme. A bunch of API accessible function modules could replace OSs now, and you just say, give me these features in a window and it does. That's effectively the same as writing a webpage.

comments.author: @KurtWoloch
comments.text: OK, one problem I see with this new way of "creating", no, "thinking out" software is that it's extremely slow, and it's also inconsistent. The LLM would have to keep the rules of the game in mind, and that's hard as its context fills up with the things that already happened. And it gets slower and slower as the context fills up. So... I think at some point the model should detect that it's doing the same thing again, such as the ball hit another brick, and then it should try to automate repeated tasks after it's done them the same way several times... by writing code for that function which does it on its own, and quicker, without the AI model having to think about it again. In the end you should have a complete, coded game that runs autonomously without needing the AI model to run anymore... or maybe it then runs on a very small version of an AI model that gets created by the big one... maybe it generates a very small AI model that only contains the inputs and outputs required for that game to run and knows nothing about the rest of the world... but it's able to run locally on your CPU and/or GPU and doesn't need the "master model" anymore. Because, if you think about it, you can interpret what the CPU the GPU doalso as "thinking", only that it "thinks" in a pre-determined way, determined by the given software and its hardware implementation, but it does so very quickly. Maybe it would even be a good idea to include an FGPA in the PC in the future, a special chip that could be reprogrammed by the AI depending on what's needed for the tasks that PC often has to do.

comments.text: Have they tried hooking the AI to a compiler? It seems feasible to me. Teaching it what runs and what doesn't. I mean... I'm not sure if that would improve anything too much. Cause when it comes to code, from what I've tested, the main issue is figuring out what you want your code to actually do. I'm not really sure that when implementing a work flow every programmer and manager really understood what they are aiming at. The famous problem of computer vision. The first time they've tried achieving that, they thought one person could do it in a few months. At least that's how the story goes. And understanding what a human wants it's most of the time really hard even for another human. Don't you think this is somewhat of an interesting philosophical question? Do you know what you want to do until someone asks you what you want to do? Because most tasks involve humans wanting things to be OK. What are you doing there? I'm making an omlet. But when I say that, I'm not referring to the action of scrambling eggs. I'm referring to the consequences of the process. Making myself happy for feeding myself, stuff like that. Nobody wants to just scramble eggs, they all want to make an omlet. What is a good code? I don't know... Did I do good writing this? Cause if you want, I can make it worse if that's good. What are my manager's priorities? He wants me to make the code run or does he want me to not make it run so that John can do it instead of me and feel good about it? A really bizarre world when you're trying to figuring out what constitutes the task at hand. But I'm under the impression that most of these problems have already been solved in books regarding quality assurance. It will be amazingly fun for people to discover that making an AI that increases revenue means having it emulate a human. Making it not that reliable, having it take breaks, making people wait, those kinds of things. Cause many issues when it comes to implementation might result from people not being able to cope with a constant flow of information. If I was a manager trying to increase my workflow thru AI, it's put a boundary at it. No more than half an hour a day per employee. That would probably make it useful as it is.
